title: The Chariot Against the Grandsire
subtitle: Krishna drives Arjuna straight at Bhishma
story:
The next morning, of all the arrows that would be shot on the field of Kurukshetra, three were aimed at the man who did not fight.

The day had opened with the armies already locked in battle. At Duryodhana's word the Kaurava host, cased in armour with standards raised, rushed against the Pandavas and their allies, and the fight that followed was fierce enough to make the hair stand on end. Chariots and elephants churned together; feathered shafts fell upon horses and upon men. At the head of the Kaurava host came Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, his great bow in hand, raining arrows on the heroes across the field — on Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, on Arjuna himself, on the ruler of the Kekayas, on Virata and Dhrishtadyumna, on the warriors of the Chedis and the Matsyas. The Pandava line wavered at his onset; horsemen and chariot-warriors fell fast, and the Pandava divisions began to fly.

Arjuna saw the grandsire and turned in anger to the man who held the reins — Krishna, his friend, who drove his chariot into every battle. "Drive to the place where the grandsire stands," he said. "This Bhishma, with his wrath kindled, will destroy my army for Duryodhana's benefit. And Drona, Kripa, Salya and Vikarna, with all of Dhritarashtra's sons behind them and this firm bowman shielding them, will slaughter the Panchalas. So I will slay Bhishma myself, for the sake of my troops."

Krishna's answer was a warning and a promise in one breath. "Be careful," he said, "for I am about to take you straight to the grandsire's car."

And he took that chariot — the one celebrated across the world, its many banners waving, its horses handsome as a flight of white cranes, the great ape roaring on its standard, bright as the sun, its rattle like the roll of thunder — and drove it straight through the Kaurava divisions and the Surasenas, the ranks falling in his path, while Arjuna came on like an angry elephant, frightening the bravest warriors and felling them with his shafts. Bhishma, ringed about by Jayadratha's warriors, by the men of the East, the Sauviras and the Kekayas, met them with all his force.

So the great car swept to a stop before the grandsire's car, and the duel began. Then Bhishma, the finest marksman of his age, struck the charioteer himself — three arrows between the breasts. Krishna, who had driven his friend into the teeth of the enemy, took the shafts without flinching and held the car steady.

Now the arrows flew between the champions. Bhishma pierced Arjuna with seventy-seven shafts; Drona struck him with twenty-five and Kripa with fifty; Duryodhana with sixty-four and Salya with nine; Drona's son with sixty, Vikarna with three, Jayadratha with nine, Sakuni with five, and Artayani with three broad-headed arrows. Pierced on every side, Arjuna did not waver, like a mountain that arrows cannot move. In return he pierced Bhishma with twenty-five arrows, Kripa with nine, Drona with sixty, Vikarna with three, Artayani with three, and Duryodhana with five. And Satyaki, Virata, Dhrishtadyumna, the sons of Draupadi and Abhimanyu closed in around him in support, while the prince of the Panchalas pressed forward against Drona.

Then Bhishma drove eighty sharp arrows into Arjuna at once, and the warriors on Duryodhana's side were greatly cheered. Arjuna, hearing the shouts of the Kaurava champions, smiled and answered them bow for bow, taking on the great car-warriors one after another. And king Duryodhana, watching his own troops give way before Arjuna and his great bow Gandiva, turned to Bhishma. "Who else," he asked, "save the grandsire of the Kurus, Drona and Karna, could have advanced against him?"

And there, between the two armies, the bright car stood where Krishna had driven it, before the grandsire's car — with three arrows still standing in the breast of the man who held the reins, who had not once turned it away.
reflection: Krishna drives the car not away from the enemy but straight at the strongest bow on the field, and takes the arrows meant for the warrior — the charioteer shields the fighter with his own body. The image of the divine driver pierced between the breasts and unmoved is the story's quiet center: protection that asks nothing back.
content_note: Battle scene with heavy casualties and arrow exchanges, described without graphic detail.
next_story_tease: But Bhishma's fury was only gathering, and soon it would bring a moment when Krishna himself left the chariot.
hero_scene: Krishna drives the great solar-effulgent chariot with its white-crane steeds and roaring ape banner straight up to Bhishma's car, and Bhishma's three arrows strike Krishna himself between the breasts while he holds the reins unmoved.
